title: Thinking aloud
objectives: Explain each quote as you make it.

screens.title: Where marks go
screens.prose: Interviewers mark the reasoning as it happens, not only the final quote. Here is a candidate's game, spoken aloud. Some lines lose marks. Look for silence before a number, a quote with no reason, a slip, or an unexplained change.

params.title: Transcript
lines: Interviewer: Make me a market on the sum of three dice.
Candidate: (twenty seconds of silence) 9 at 12.
Interviewer: Why 9 at 12?
Candidate: Three dice average 3.5 each, so fair is 10.5. I go 1.5 either side.
Interviewer: I buy 1 at 12.
Candidate: Then 10 at 13.
Interviewer: The first die shows a 6.
Candidate: Fair is 6 plus 2 times 3.5, which is 13.5, so I quote 12 at 15.
Interviewer: I sell you 2 at 12.
Candidate: Long 1 now. Fair is 14, so 12.5 at 15.5.
Interviewer: Thank you. We will stop there.

screens.question: Tap every line that loses marks.

hints.text: Read only the candidate's lines. Which give a number with no reason?
Line 4 is the model: a fair value, its arithmetic and a width.
Lines 2, 6, 8 and 10 each lose marks: silence, no reason, a slip, an unexplained change.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Check each candidate line for a reason, correct arithmetic and an announced fair value.

byKey.good: You tapped line 4 too. It states the fair value, its arithmetic and the width: full marks.
byKey.l4: Line 4 states the fair value, its arithmetic and the width. That is what scores.

explain.text: Line 2 is silence then a bare quote, and line 6 moves with no reason. Line 8 says $6 + 7 = 13.5$, and line 10 changes fair to 14 without a word. Line 4 is the pattern to copy.

screens.title: The slip
screens.prose: Line 8 has an arithmetic slip. The first die shows 6 and two dice are still to roll.

screens.title: The P&L they never said
screens.prose: The candidate never stated a P&L. Rebuild the ledger and mark it at the true fair value, 13.
screens.question: What is the candidate's P&L at fair after line 9, in pounds?

hints.text: Add the cash to the position marked at 13.
Cash is $12 - 24 = -12$. Long 1 is worth 13.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Cash plus position times 13.

byKey.slip: You marked at 13.5, the slipped fair value.
byKey.fourteen: You marked at 14, the fair value the candidate changed to without a reason.
byKey.cash: That is the cash alone. Add the long 1 at 13.

explain.text: Cash is $+12 - 24 = -12$ and long 1 is worth 13, so the P&L is +£1. Interviewers ask for it after every trade. Saying it unprompted shows you track risk as you go.

screens.title: Two ways to say it
screens.prose: The interviewer asks for a market on the sum of two dice. Four candidates answer.

params.title: Transcript

screens.question: Which answer earns the most marks?

options.text: "Two dice average 3.5 each, so fair is 7. The roll could land far off, so I will go 2 wide: 6 at 8."
"Somewhere around 7, maybe, so roughly 6 to 8, I think."

Look for the words that explain each number.
The answer that averages 3.5 per die gives 7, then a width of 2 for the spread of the roll.

feedback.correct: The one with every number and its reason.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Look for a fair value, its arithmetic and a reason for the width.

byKey.vague: You hedged every word. A range with no stated fair value or reason sounds unsure, not careful.
byKey.precise: You chose false precision. A width of 0.02 on a roll that varies by 2.4 ignores the risk.
byKey.sorry: You apologised instead of reasoning. The quote is fine, but nothing in it can be marked.

screens.title: The order of a first quote
screens.prose: A first quote has a natural order. Each sentence uses the one before it.
screens.question: Put the sentences in the order you would say them.

lines.text: "A market on the sum of three dice, settled at the roll."
"The total has an sd of about 3, so I want some width."
"I will quote 9.5 at 11.5, 2 wide, for 1 lot."
"If you trade, I will say why I move."

hints.text: What must you have before you can quote?
The fair value comes before the width, and the width before the quote.
Question back, fair value, uncertainty, quote, then what you will do next.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Each sentence should rest on the one before it.

explain.text: Stating the question back catches a misheard game. The fair value and the width are the two numbers a quote is built from. The last line tells the interviewer you will keep reasoning aloud.

screens.title: Silent but right
screens.prose: A candidate thinks in silence for forty seconds, then gives the perfect quote: "9.5 at 11.5." Nothing else.

screens.title: Interrupted
screens.prose: You are mid-sentence: "The first die is a 6, so fair is 6 plus...". The interviewer cuts in: "I buy 2 at your ask." You quote with half-width 1 and skew 0.25 a lot.
screens.question: What do you say next?

options.text: "...6 plus 7, so 13. You bought 2: I am short 2. Moving up to 12.5 at 14.5."
"Short 2. 11 at 13."
options.why: You dropped the update. The fair value moved with the 6, so your new quote rests on nothing said.

options.text: "...6 plus 7, so 13." and wait
options.why: You finished the update but ignored the trade. Say the new position and requote.

options.text: "Sorry, can we start again?"
options.why: You stopped the game. Interruptions are part of it: finish the thought, then answer the trade.

hints.text: Two things are pending: the fair value and the trade.
Finish the sentence first, then take the trade.
Say 13, then short 2, then the new quote with its reason.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Finish the fair value, then answer the trade.

byKey.drop: You dropped the update. The fair value moved with the 6, so your new quote rests on nothing said.
byKey.ignore: You finished the update but ignored the trade. Say the new position and requote.

explain.text: Finish the update so the fair value is on record, then answer the trade. Short 2 with fair 13 and a skew of 0.25 a lot puts the centre at 13.5. A half-width of 1 then gives 12.5 at 14.5.

screens.title: Every number with its reason
screens.prose:
A spoken quote is the skew rule read aloud, one term at a time:
$$m = F - \gamma q, \qquad \text{bid} = m - h, \quad \text{ask} = m + h.$$
Say $F$ with its arithmetic, $q$ after each trade, $m$ with the skew, and the width $2h$ with its reason.
screens.question: Fair 10.5, long 2, skew 0.5 a lot. What centre do you say?

hints.text: Long means $q = +2$.
$\gamma q = 0.5 \times 2 = 1$.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Subtract $\gamma q$ from the fair value.

byKey.sign: You moved up. A long lowers the centre, to sell more easily.
byKey.flat: You left out the skew for the 2 lots you hold.

explain.text: "Fair 10.5, long 2, skewing 0.5 a lot, so I centre at 9.5." One sentence carries every term. Each number has its reason attached.

screens.title: Flags in code
screens.prose: A simple rule finds some lost marks: a line with a number but no word of reason. Code it, then see what it misses on the candidate's five lines.
screens.question: Complete `transcript_flags`.

widget.starter:
REASONS = ("because", "so", "since", "from")


def transcript_flags(lines):
    """Indices (0-based) of lines that contain a digit
    but none of the words in REASONS (case ignored,
    whole words only)."""
    ...
widget.solution:
REASONS = ("because", "so", "since", "from")


def transcript_flags(lines):
    """Indices (0-based) of lines that contain a digit
    but none of the words in REASONS (case ignored,
    whole words only)."""
    out = []
    for i, line in enumerate(lines):
        has_digit = any(ch.isdigit() for ch in line)
        words = "".join(c if c.isalpha() else " " for c in line.lower()).split()
        if has_digit and not any(w in REASONS for w in words):
            out.append(i)
    return out

tests.setup: cand = ['(twenty seconds of silence) 9 at 12.', 'Three dice average 3.5 each, so fair is 10.5. I go 1.5 either side.', 'Then 10 at 13.', 'Fair is 6 plus 2 times 3.5, which is 13.5, so I quote 12 at 15.', 'Long 1 now. Fair is 14, so 12.5 at 15.5.']

tests.call: transcript_flags(['I move up because I am short 2.'])

widget.how: Check runs 8 hidden tests, including the candidate's five lines. A reason word must match as a whole word: "also" is not "so".

hints.text: Split each line into lower-case words of letters only.
"Also" must not count as "so": compare whole words.
Flag line `i` when it has a digit and no word in `REASONS`.

feedback.generic: Some tests failed. Match reason words as whole words, ignoring case.

byKey.error: Your code stopped with an error. Check that `...` is replaced.

explain.text: The rule flags the silent quote and the bare move. It misses the slip and the unexplained change to 14, because both contain "so". A keyword finds missing reasons; only a listener finds wrong ones.

screens.title: A first round
screens.prose: A real trader interview's first round often opens like this. Two dice, fair 7, your quote 6 at 8. The interviewer says: "I buy 3 at 8."
screens.question: Which reply scores best?

options.text: "Short 3 at 8; at fair 7 I am up £3. A buyer may know something and I am short, so I move up: 7 at 9."

options.why: You gave the new quote with no position, P&L or reason. Each of those is a mark.

options.text: "Short 3, up £3. I move down to sell more: 5 at 7."
options.why: You moved the wrong way. Short 3 wants to buy back, so the quote moves up.

options.text: "Short 3, up £3. I stay at 6 at 8."
options.why: You ignored the trade. A buyer is information and your short is risk; both say move up.

hints.text: Say the position, the P&L, and the reason for the move.
Short 3 at 8 against fair 7 is +£3.
Both the information and the inventory say move up.

feedback.correct: Position, P&L, reason, then the quote.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Say the position and P&L, then move up with the reason.

byKey.bare: You gave the new quote with no position, P&L or reason. Each of those is a mark.
byKey.down: You moved the wrong way. Short 3 wants to buy back, so the quote moves up.

explain.text: Short 3 sold at 8 against fair 7 is +£3. A buyer may be informed and the short is risk, so the quote moves up. Saying all four in one breath is what a first round rewards.

screens.title: Your spoken game
screens.prose: Homework 3 asks you to play a full game aloud, about ten minutes, kept with a watch. Then you write it out and mark it against a 10-point rubric. There is no recording: be your own listener.
screens.question: Select all that apply: what must your narrated game contain?

options.text: The fair value with its arithmetic, after every card
Each quote's width with its reason
The position and P&L after every trade
An apology when you are unsure
options.why: You apologised. Say what you are unsure of as a width instead.

options.text: A silent pause before each number, to be safe
options.why: You kept silent. A pause filled with your working scores; a silent one does not.

hints.text: Which items can an interviewer mark?
Numbers with their reasons can be marked.
Fair values, widths with reasons, and the ledger after each trade.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Choose the items that put reasoning on record.

byKey.sorry: You apologised. Say what you are unsure of as a width instead.
byKey.pause: You kept silent. A pause filled with your working scores; a silent one does not.

explain.text: The rubric marks fair values, widths with reasons, the response to each trade and the ledger. Apologies and silence earn nothing. Practise with a watch so ten minutes feels normal.

ideas: Interviewers mark the reasoning as it happens: say every number with its reason.
A first quote runs: the question back, the fair value with arithmetic, the uncertainty, the quote and its width.
After a trade, say the position and P&L first, then the move and why; finish an interrupted update before requoting.

quiz.question: What do you say first?

options.text: "Long 1 at 6, up £1 at fair 7."

options.why: You requoted before stating the trade. Position and P&L come first.

options.text: "Why did you sell?"
options.why: You asked the interviewer to reason for you. Say what the trade means to you.

options.text: "Sorry, I priced that badly."
options.why: You apologised for a trade with £1 of edge. Say the P&L instead.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. State the new position and P&L before anything else.

explain.text: Long 1 bought at 6 against fair 7 is +£1. Saying it first shows you track the ledger. The new quote and its reason come next.

quiz.prose: Three cards from a full deck, ace 1 to king 13. The first card shows a 10.
quiz.question: What fair value do you say for the sum?

feedback.generic: Not quite right. The other two cards average $354/51$.

byKey.seven: You used 7 for each unseen card. The 10 is gone, so they average $354/51 = 6.94$.
byKey.all: You kept the fair value from before the card.

explain.text: The deck holds $364 - 10 = 354$ points in 51 cards. Two unseen cards average $2 \times 354/51 = 13.88$, so fair is 23.88. Say the 354 and the 51 aloud.

quiz.prose: You need ten seconds to work out a fair value.
quiz.question: What do you do with those ten seconds?

options.text: Work it out aloud, step by step
Stay silent, then give the answer
options.why: You hid the working. The interviewer cannot mark what they do not hear.

options.text: Give a guess now and fix it later
options.why: You guessed. A number with no reason scores less than the working that finds it.

options.text: Ask for more time
options.why: You paused the game. Ten seconds of spoken working needs no permission.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Spend the time saying your working.

explain.text: Ten seconds of spoken working is ten seconds of marks. A slip said aloud can be caught and fixed. Silence earns nothing.
